column1: Courtesy of the artistI remember the first time I heard someone refer to the Tiny Desk as “an iconic space.” Someone was giving a tour of the NPR offices — this was back before the company moved into the building where we now work

column1: When suggesting a price to a client
column2: I usually do a comparative market analysis to get a sense of what similar properties have recently sold for. I even take my client to other currently listed properties in their area and show them the pluses and minuses of a property compared to their own.

column2: I advise we price it a little below what we think the property is worth but do an offer date — only accepting offers on one day — and see what the market will offer. This sales strategy is often done in hot sellers’ markets and when it is hard to price a property because it is unique.

What to know about the six leading mayoral candidates
The race to replace John Tory is now a crowded but focused affair. Crowded because now that registrations are closed
column2: we know there are a record 102 mayoral candidates
column3: their names set in virtual stone. Mail-in ballots look like a small-print page from a big city phone book. Focused because opinion polling from three different firms identify the same leading contenders: ex-police chief Mark Saunders
column5: ex-Liberal MPP Mitzie Hunter
column6: ex-NDP MP Olivia Chow
column7: Coun. Brad Bradford and ex-councillor Ana Bailão.

column1: Those polls — showing Chow the frontrunner by a significant margin
column2: usually with Saunders and Matlow next in line — likely reflect those candidates’ high name recognition. Change is likely. Now that we’re in debate season — there were three on Wednesday alone — potential voters should start to tune in and get a sense of the people and their policies
column3: and an idea of what they could do for Toronto’s future rather than just memories of what they’ve done in the past.

column1: With one month until most people vote on June 26
column2: here is a subjective look at each of the front-runners
column3: how they are positioning themselves and the challenges they face.

column1: Ana Bailão: Council’s former housing advocate inherited much of Tory’s former team. She has raised the most money the quickest and will advertise heavily. She needs a boost in name recognition because polling numbers often place her fourth or fifth. She has positioned herself as a housing expert who can get Premier Doug Ford to upload Toronto’s highways. Ford
column3: shot that idea down. With the electorate seemingly in the mood for change
column4: Bailão’s Tory ties might not help her.

column1: Brad Bradford: Council’s planning and housing chair is also a former Tory ally fighting to get name recognition and stand out from the pack. He has positioned himself as a “strong mayor of action” poised to blast through bureaucracy to get housing built
column2: transit made safe and more. There’s little evidence it’s working yet
column4: and his aggressive debate demeanour could turn off voters.

column1: Olivia Chow: Some political observers are surprised at her apparent lead given she hasn’t been in elected politics for eight years. Skeptics note Chow’s early lead in the 2014 mayoral election evaporated. But the vote is not far away and her positioning — an unabashedly progressive leader with a depth of experience — could catch a public mood. Her sometimes fuzzy answers
column3: give an opening to rivals’ attacks that will only intensify.

column1: Mitzie Hunter: The Scarborough politician is likeable
column2: smart and has rolled out significant policies. She would make history as Toronto’s first Black mayor. Her challenge is to raise her profile and define her progressive message — to “fix the Six” — in a way that vaults her ahead of left-leaning rivals Chow and Matlow
column3: who are better known in civic circles.

column1: Josh Matlow: The midtown councillor is running against Ford as much as his mayoral rivals. A past Tory nemesis
column2: he is vowing to abandon Toronto’s “get along to go along” approach to Queen’s Park and fight the interventionist premier to fix the city’s finances
column3: build housing and more. He has lots of thoughtful policy but Chow seems to have pulled ahead as the progressive choice. Matlow’s pointed debate quips ensure he’s quoted
column4: but won’t help dispel talk that he’s not a team player.

column1: Mark Saunders: The ex-police chief is trying to portray his lack of political experience as an asset
column2: blaming rivals for all of Toronto’s ills that can be fixed only by his leadership. Saunders is running from the right
column3: hitting hard on voters’ fear of crime and blaming bike lanes for aggravating traffic gridlock. His challenge is to convince voters that close ties to Ford are an asset
column4: and rebut challenges to his record as the city’s top cop.

column1: That’s the race as it stands — but
column3: this is Toronto politics. There are 102 reasons it could all change.

Standout office lunches within the PATH
My colleagues and I recently explored how hybrid work has changed downtown Toronto. I wrote about how the lunchtime crowd is slowly returning to the city’s core
column2: and Katie Daubs looked into the state of the PATH
column3: the city’s underground labyrinth that spans more than 30 kilometres. It boasts lots of food options — so if you’ve returned to work downtown
column4: here are some great spots for lunch or a midday treat.

column1: The teriyaki tofu from Ho Ga Oriental Cuisine
Ho Ga Oriental Cuisine is one of the few independent food stalls in the PATH. It’s in one of the smaller food courts
column2: but it’s hardly a secret. Even on quiet days
column3: there’s a line down the hall because this longstanding Korean-Japanese spot offers lunch boxes that cost less than $9. Due to the pandemic
column4: the menu has been pared down to seven items
column5: but it’s still a solid roster of staples like bulgogi and teriyaki.

column1: The teriyaki tofu is a hefty meal: four slabs of firm tofu in a thick batter with a light teriyaki sauce
column2: served over steamed rice with a choice of two sides. I opted for the kimchi slaw — it’s slightly astringent
column3: but less spicy than regular kimchi — and jap chae
column4: Korean glass noodles. It's a comforting home-cooked meal that's the closest you'll get to bringing a packed lunch.

column1: Ho Ga is in the 121 King St. W. building (just east of York Street) in the lower level. Like all food stalls in the PATH
column2: it’s only open on weekdays. It’s a small mom-and-pop operation
column3: so it’s not on delivery apps.

column1: The Oaxaca bowl from Kupfert and Kim When Kupfert and Kim opened its first location a decade ago
column2: my coworkers were ecstatic about having a fully vegan lunch spot in the downtown core. Since day one
column3: I’ve ordered the Oaxaca bowl: a bed of brown rice
column5: black beans
column6: cashew crème
column7: pico de gallo
column8: guacamole
column9: sliced radish
column10: beets
column11: tortilla chips and lime wedges. It’s the ideal office worker lunch — it’s filling
column12: full of vegetables and has a nice balance of protein and carbs to get you through the day without wanting a nap. The cashew crème is a nutty
column13: creamy sauce that pairs well with the nutty brown rice
column14: while the acidity in the pico de gallo helps cut the kale’s bitterness. The bowl costs $14.75
column15: which is on par for a PATH food court lunch nowadays
column16: but in terms of size and number of ingredients
column17: it’s one of the better value meals.

column1: Kupfert and Kim has multiple locations in the PATH. They each have different hours — some are open until 10 p.m. All the locations have the same menu
column2: but my favourite location is in the RBC Waterpark Place upstairs food court at 20 Bay St. (at Queens Quay West). The food court has reliable free WiFi and lots of natural light
column3: and it’s close to Scotiabank Arena. You can find a directory of all locations and order online on its website.

column1: The classic peppercorn steak from Jump Restaurant Jump has been a reliable lunch and dinner spot for decades. Though it may seem better suited for high-powered execs with money to spend
column2: the menu prices are a little more affordable than you’d expect for what you’re getting (especially for a fine-dining restaurant in the heart of the Financial District). At $36
column3: the 8 oz peppercorn sirloin coulotte — a lean cut from the sirloin tip — with frites is a reasonable lunch splurge. If you’re here for dinner
column4: the alternative is a $52 7 oz tenderloin. My medium-rare steak was cooked perfectly
column5: and the green peppercorn jus added a rich astringent contrast. The fries are delicately crisp
column6: and it also comes with a side of grilled broccolini.

column1: Jump is on the street level of Commerce Court at 18 Wellington St. W. (right between Yonge and Bay streets). Reservations are highly recommended during the weekday lunch rush between noon and 2 p.m. — otherwise you can try your luck at the bar. There isn’t a strict dress code
column2: but the crowd is all navy suits so you might want to at least go for business casual attire.

column1: The snickerdoodle cookie from Maman During the mid-afternoon coffee runs you’ll see a flood of office workers clutching blue and white cups from Maman
column2: this New York-based café and bakery. The lattes are on par with the third-wave espresso bars you can find elsewhere in the core
column3: but it’s the cookies that are worth coming back for. The snickerdoodle one is made with plant-based butter
column4: making it one of the rare vegan baked goods in the PATH that isn’t the typical coconut-date concoction. It has a crisp exterior rolled in cinnamon sugar
column5: while the inside is chewy and moist. The cookies are sized quite generously
column6: so one is big enough to nibble on throughout the day
column7: and it costs $4.50.

column1: Maman is in First Canadian Place’s upstairs food court at 100 King St. W.
column2: between Bay and York streets. It’s open on weekdays from 8 a.m. to around 2:30 p.m. Its hours are on its website
column3: and you can order online through Uber Eats.

column1: What we know about the health risks of ultra-processed foods

column3: the frozen tater tots come with additional calories: fat (from vegetable oil)

column7: stabilizers and dyes used in so-called “ultra-processed foods.”

column2: 20 healthy adult volunteers stayed at an NIH facility for four weeks. For two weeks
column3: volunteers were fed a diet of ultra-processed foods: meals like canned beef ravioli
column4: chicken salad made with canned chicken
column5: tater tots and hot dogs. Then for the next two weeks
column6: they ate minimally processed foods: mainly fruits
column7: vegetables and unprocessed meat. Each diet had essentially the same total amount of fat
column8: sugar
column9: salt
column10: fiber

column2: but in our home summer is a time to slooooooow down. The kids are home and creating chaos

column4: and time just seems to move a little differently. I wouldn't have it any other way - I love to soak up every minute I can of their time off! But

column6: I sat down this week to write out a quick list of 5 things I want to do around the house this summer. Just five! It's low pressure

column9: I can call it a wildly successful summer. Here's my summer project list. (I'd love to know what's on yours if you decide to make one

column16: and the vision is still coming together

column1: Abortion Is Already Tripping Up The 2024 Republican Candidates
Ask six Republican candidates for president whether they think there should be a national ban on abortion
column2: and you’ll get at least seven different answers. In just the past two months
column3: current and prospective candidates have committed at various points to the general idea of a federal bans on abortion (maybe 15 weeks of pregnancy)
column4: said it’s a states’ rights issue but they’re looking at “alternatives
column5: ” expressed support for six-week bans at the state level while declining to say whether they think a national version would be appropriate
column6: and said they support efforts to get a widely used abortion drug “off the market.”

column1: All of this waffling might suggest that the Republican Party is struggling to find a path forward on abortion after last year’s midterm elections
column2: where abortion rights was a drag on GOP candidates in swing states. But something more complicated is happening. Republicans passed a significant number of first-trimester restrictions at the state level this spring
column3: ranging from full bans to bans on abortion after 12 weeks of pregnancy
column4: none of which are popular with most Americans. And many of the GOP candidates are coalescing around some form of national ban
column5: even if they aren’t on the same page about the specifics.

column1: So the GOP isn’t backing down on its efforts to restrict abortion
column2: even in the face of fairly broad public opposition. The dispute now — in state legislatures and among the presidential candidates — is more about how far to go and how quickly. Presidential candidates are in a tough spot — caught between state legislatures
column3: courts intervening in unexpected ways and unambiguously negative polling numbers on abortion restrictions. That’s particularly true for higher-polling candidates like former President Donald Trump and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis
column4: who need to weigh how a gung-ho attitude about abortion restrictions — while probably helpful during the primary — would play in a general election. Read more

In my first few months as NPR’s Public Editor
column2: I received a flurry of notes about a joke on Wait Wait… Don’t Tell Me! that didn’t go over well. The executive producer at the time responded to my email with something like
column3: Nice to meet you. Since we’re a comedy show
column4: we will probably come to your attention about once a year. We’re always happy to talk.

column1: That prediction was spot on. I’ve just finished my third year in the office and we’re on our third newsletter item about Wait Wait. We’ve addressed a joke about chicken slapping in 2021 that drew objections of animal cruelty from bird lovers. And in early 2022
column2: a joke about former comedian and current Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy being “used to bombing” did not go over well. Now we have a joke that involved a reference to the Holocaust
column3: but was not about the Holocaust. It was about Taco Bell. But it did mention the Holocaust and that will almost always inspire ire.

column1: Read on to see the details of the joke and how it came to be.

column2: we appreciate the balance that Wait Wait brings to the diversity of shows NPR offers. Frankly
column3: it seems right that a comedy show about the news would test boundaries every once in a while. The folks who work on the show always respond to our questions and explain their process. In a weird way
column4: we look forward to chatting with them.

column1: Here are a few quotes from the Public Editor's inbox that resonated with us. Letters are edited for length and clarity. You can share your questions and concerns with us through the NPR Contact page.

Patty Rich Zucherman wrote on May 21: I was greatly disturbed by what was said on Wait Wait today ... regarding the Taco Bell reference “Taco Holocaust Remembrance Day.” This reference to the Holocaust along with Taco Bell was insensitive
column4: and terribly harmful in making comedy of the Holocaust. I am greatly disappointed and shocked by this choice of writing. …I was taken aback when I heard this joke
column5: as well. For those who missed it
column6: here’s the background: During a Wait Wait… Don’t Tell Me! show recorded on May 18 with a live audience at the Studebaker Theater in Chicago
column7: host Peter Sagal asked panel members several questions based on the week’s news. He asked panelist Negin Farsad: “Taco Bell and the less well-known chain Taco John’s are in a heated legal dispute right now over who gets to use what phrase?”

column1: The answer: the popular phrase “Taco Tuesday.”

column3: “It turns out that the restaurant Taco John’s trademarked the phrase Taco Tuesday back in 1989. But Taco Bell has filed to get that trademark lifted so they can use it
column5: right? Taco Tuesday — it’s a natural. They’re just mad because all of their trademark days never caught on. What were they thinking with Taco Holocaust Remembrance Day?”

column2: executive producer of Wait Wait whether he felt the joke worked.

column1: “Sort of! It got the kind of boo/laugh response we were expecting
column2: ” he told us in an email. “It’s an edgy joke
column3: making fun of corporations and their misguided attempts to create brands and trademarks around specific days/events.

column1: “We definitely think very hard about the jokes we make. In this case
column2: the joke was about Taco Bell doing something dumb
column3: ” Danforth continued. “I can totally understand how someone would not find it funny.”

column1: That’s me. I understand the joke’s suggestion that companies sometimes trademark ridiculous things. But the mention of the Holocaust was distracting and disconcerting. — Amaris Castillo

column1: 2034;Chimp Empire and the Economics of Chimpanzees;"A new Netflix docuseries provides a fascinating picture of humanity’s closest living relatives.

Chimponomicsby Greg RosalskyWatching Netflix’s new docuseries Chimp Empire is a trip. It feels like being dropped in the middle of the Ugandan forest and suddenly becoming roommates with chimpanzees. It’s incredibly immersive. You get to know the chimps as individuals
column2: each with their own personalities and goals. And you get a glimpse of the inner workings of chimp society
column3: complete with its fluid hierarchies and deadly power struggles.

column1: Chimp Empire was filmed over a year in Uganda’s Kibale National Park. The filmmakers embedded themselves with the Ngogo chimpanzees
column2: the largest known chimpanzee society. While these chimps once lived in relative peace and harmony
column3: they now have split into two warring clans
column4: which scientists refer to as the Central and Western factions.

column2: what’s particularly fascinating about this conflict is that economics seems to be at the center of it. The Central and Western chimp clans are competing for the ownership of a scarce resource: fruit trees
column3: which are their primary source of sustenance. At the beginning of the series
column4: the Central chimps have control over some of the most coveted fruit trees. They even patrol their borders to ensure that the Western Chimps don’t encroach on them. But — without giving away too much — the Western Chimps do exactly that
column5: and the territorial conflict turns violent.

column1: The apes in Chimp Empire also display other behaviors that are interesting from an economic perspective. Alpha males use the spoils from their group’s hunts strategically
column2: giving meat to allies while excluding those who pose a threat to their dominance. The chimps also engage in a kind of grooming barter system. Ticks and other parasites are a serious problem in the jungle
column3: and the chimps spend hours grooming each other to ensure that they don’t get sick. It’s literally you scratch my back
column5: in the docuseries
column6: there are stories of low-ranking chimps grooming higher-ranking chimps but not getting groomed in exchange. In this way
column7: this grooming barter system communicates power
column8: kinship
column9: and rank.

column3: are our closest relatives in the natural world. Scientists have compared their DNA to ours
column4: and they find that more than 98 percent of our genetic code is identical. Research suggests that humans and chimps both share a common ancestor species
column5: and
column6: somewhere between six and nine million years ago
column7: we diverged and started evolving into the distinct creatures we are today.

column1: Given our primal connection to chimpanzees
column2: social scientists have long been interested in our behavioral similarities and differences — including when it comes to our economic behavior. By understanding how this more primitive species behaves
column4: maybe we can gain a better understanding of how humans behaved in the ancient past
column5: and how we’ve evolved and changed with civilization.

column1: Chimpo Economicus In the classic model of neoclassical economics
column2: human beings are portrayed as selfish creatures who always do the best that they can to maximize their own wealth and happiness. The model assumes that people are rational
column3: meaning that they will logically pursue their goals and not get systematically tripped up by their quirks
column5: or emotions. Economists call this stylized version of humans homo economicus.

column2: the field of behavioral economics has shone a bright spotlight on the fact that human beings often don’t behave like homo economicus. They engage in all sorts of behaviors that can result in them failing to maximize their own wealth or happiness. Sometimes they do so because of irrationality
column3: or errors in their thinking. Other times they do so because they choose to do so. For example
column5: perhaps because of innate empathy or socialization
column6: tend to be more generous and altruistic than the crude
column7: simplified economic model of the past suggests we are. And
column8: this
column9: evolutionarily speaking
column10: makes a lot of sense. We are
column11: after all
column12: a social species: the more we cooperate
column13: the more we thrive.

column1: With this model of behavior in mind
column2: social scientists have long been interested in researching whether chimps are more or less selfish than humans. For decades
column3: researchers conducted lab experiments with chimps that suggested they were
column5: almost completely selfish. They found in laboratory experiments that chimps tended to hoard food and were unwilling to hand over snacks to fellow apes
column6: even when it didn’t really cost them anything. This made it seem like maybe kindness and concern for others was more of a human trait
column7: and that chimps were closer to the crude model of selfish homo economicus than we are.

column2: more recent experiments have found that
column4: chimps are actually more generous than once thought
column5: and even that they are more social and evolved than selfish homo economicus. In one experiment
column6: researchers Michael Tomasello and Felix Warneken put two chimps in two different rooms. Both primates had a clear view of mouth-watering fruit in a third room. The scientists gave one chimp the capability to open the door for the other chimp to go and get the fruit
column7: even though the chimp with control over the door wouldn’t get to feast. The researchers found that the chimp opened the door for the other chimp around 80% of the time. Pretty generous!

column1: Other studies have found similar behaviors. Chimps warn their compatriots about imminent dangers. They give tools to their compatriots when they request them. So while humans may be more generous than apes
column2: researchers find that concern for others is not a uniquely human trait.

column1: The Endowment EffectChimpanzees also display some of the same quirks that humans do. Behavioral economists have long found that humans
column3: tend to value an object more after they have gained possession of it. For example
column4: we might think a coffee mug is worth only $5 when we buy it at the store. Then
column5: after we buy it
column6: we value it more. Someone could offer us like $8 or $9 for it. But
column7: we’re like
column8: “No way! This is my precious mug!” From a purely rational economic perspective
column9: this behavior doesn’t make sense.

column3: called this tendency to value things in our possession more “the endowment effect.” He connected it to a broader human quirk
column4: which is called loss aversion. The basic idea is that we experience more pain from losing something than pleasure from gaining that exact same thing. We see this behavior everywhere
column5: whether it’s our romantic relationships or our consumer decisions. You may sort of like getting something
column6: but you’ll really hate losing it!

column1: What’s interesting is that a group of researchers has found that chimpanzees exhibit the exact same behavioral quirk
column2: particularly when it comes to food. “These findings suggest that many seeming deviations from rational choice predictions may be common to humans and chimpanzees and that the evaluation of these through a lens of evolutionary relevance may yield further insights in humans and other species

column5: and civilization
column6: chimps aren’t so different from us after all. At the very least
column7: we’re both much more interesting
column8: social
column9: and quirky than the creatures portrayed in old-school economic textbooks.

column2: we’re officially at 2023’s midway point. Instead of celebrating with champagne and sequins
column3: it’s time to check in on the New Year’s resolutions you set six months ago. If that makes you a tad anxious…same

column2: most of my New Year’s resolutions have not survived the spring. My Duolingo streak has evaporated
column3: my sleep is still dysregulated and my savings account is less flush than I would like. Alas. Expecting instant — and significant — behavior shifts from ourselves is usually an exercise in futility.

column1: But here’s the thing: I love resolutions
column2: and I’ll probably never stop making them. It gives me a chance to reflect on and affirm my values. Even if I won’t be hitting a 365-day Duolingo streak anytime soon (perdóname
column4: I still care about learning Spanish. I’ve been watching The Heist on Netflix and practicing speaking with my sisters when I can. I’m not reaching my goal of eight or more hours of sleep each night
column5: but I’m still trying. Lately I’ve been reading before bed instead of scrolling Instagram
column6: and I like to think it helps.

column1: If I frame resolutions as part of my self-growth
column2: I'm allowed to pivot. And halfway through the year is a great time to recommit to those goals — or pick new ones entirely. For example
column3: perfecting my sunscreen routine has moved up my priority list.

column10: joy
column11: escape

column3: another small-town kid is turning on country radio in 2023 and experiencing the same world-expanding cocktail of wonder and discovery that I did.

2159;Toronto’s most unique ice cream flavours;"Food Crawl
Four scoops you can’t find anywhere else
It’s officially ice cream season. My colleague Manuela Vega rounded up 10 must-visit spots
column2: and I found four more places that offer unique flavours you can’t find anywhere else — quite a feat considering how many ice cream shops Toronto has. Wherever you are in the city
column3: I’ve got you covered for a one-of-a kind spin on the quintessential summertime treat.

column1: The pei pa koa half pint from Onyx Chocolates
This East Chinatown chocolate shop has some of the most creative ice cream flavours around. The pei pa koa caught my eye — the Chinese herbal tonic with honey
column3: licorice and peppermint will either elicit shivers or glee from generations of kids who were given it to soothe a sore throat. It doesn’t have any actual medical ingredients
column4: but it’s like swallowing a spoonful of minty honey with a bittersweet
column5: grassy and slightly bitter citrus peel finish.

column2: ribbons of pei pa koa add a herbaceous layer to a plain vanilla base
column3: and swirls of caramel further offset the tonic’s flavour. Other standout flavours include ying-yeung — a Hong Kong drink of half milk tea
column4: half coffee — and five spice salted caramel. Onyx also sells chocolate bonbons
column5: which I’ve previously recommended in Food Crawl. Here’s more about their innovative flavours
column6: including pei pa koa.

column1: Onyx Chocolates is at 601 Gerrard St. E.
column2: just east of Broadview Avenue. It’s closed Mondays and Tuesdays. The ice cream is sold in half and full pints rather than scoops
column3: and a half pint (8 oz.) serving is about $8. Dairy-free and vegan options are available. The ice cream isn’t available on delivery apps
column4: but bonbons can be shipped within the city.

column1: The avocado mint cone from The Chocolateria This little chocolate shop on the Roncesvalles strip offers an unconventional flavour combo: avocado and mint. Other avocado-flavoured desserts I’ve tried tend to be muted
column2: but in this cone you can distinctly taste the buttery
column3: slightly nutty quality of the fruit along with refreshing mint. The combo works well if you’re craving something subtle and outside of the usual chocolate and vanilla options.

column1: The Chocolateria is at 361 Roncesvalles Ave.
column2: south of Neepawa Avenue. A single scoop in a plain cone is about $4. You can order pints in advance for pickup through its site. Dairy-free options are available.

column1: The yuzu cheesecake gelato from Gelato North A Twitter follower tipped me off to Gelato North
column2: and it’s worth the trek up to the city’s northern edge. The easy-to-miss gelato shop is owned by a South Korean and Italian couple
column3: resulting in flavours like black sesame
column4: tiramisu and caramel macchiato. Their newest flavour
column5: yuzu cheesecake
column6: is incredibly rich
column7: with small bits of candied yuzu peel in a light syrup. It reminds me of my favourite no-nonsense New York cheesecake from Veniero’s. The yuzu cheesecake flavour also made it to the North American semifinals of this year’s Gelato World Masters (yep
column8: it’s a real thing).

column1: Gelato North is at 5510 Yonge St.
column2: just south of Finch Avenue East. You can order takeout through Uber Eats and SkipTheDishes on its site. Dairy-free and vegan options are available. It’s open every day from 1 p.m. until 11 p.m.
column3: except Mondays when it closes at 10 p.m. A small scoop in a waffle cone is about $7.

column1: The Torta Della Nonna cone from Good Behaviour  Good Behaviour offers dinner and dessert in one spot. I recommended its caprese sub in a past edition of Food Crawl
column3: finish with a generous scoop of Torta Della Nonna. It’s a tart
column4: creamy lemon ricotta flavour with bits of shortbread and pine nuts
column5: which add a savoury crunch to the not-too-sweet scoop. I’ve been told the Torta Della Nonna’s not-overly saccharine flavour is part of its appeal. Good Behaviour’s ice cream flavours rotate (alas
column6: the more adventurous cacio e pepe with actual pecorino and black pepper was not available when I visited)
column7: but as one of the original flavours
column8: this one is more of a sure shot.

column1: Good Behaviour has two locations. One is in the west end along the strip of restaurants on Geary Avenue (it’s on a corner spot at 342 Westmoreland Ave. N.). The newer
column2: larger location is in Leslieville at 1324A Gerrard St E.
column4: and it also sells snacks and prepared foods from other local makers. Both locations are open daily from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m.
column5: and you can order through Ritual via its site. A single scoop in a waffle cone is about $7. Dairy-free and vegan options are available.

The overall assignment was to ""do something with evolutionary
algorithms.""  The goal of my project was more or less to attack a
spam filter and attempt to use an EA to find weaknesses it might
have.  I set up a blind watchmaker sort of natural selection/
evolution environment using a SpamBayes filter that I had trained on
an old training corpus as the fitness function.  The program I wrote
attempted to evolve a generic formula that worked sort of like
MadLibs"" to write spam emails that could get past the filter.  I
started off with almost zero knowledge of how a spam filter works

would be as naive as possible.  I've since read up on SpamBayes and

Here are test patches which should be of interest to this who've been having problems with the I/O speed. I'm providing patches for 2.6.23.15 and 2.6.24.1. The whole lowlevel I/O code has had quite a rework. In /sys/power/tuxonice/block_io
column9: the only remaining entry is target_outstanding_io
column10: which can be used to say how much memory you'd like to have made available for I/O. If more is available
column11: it will be used too. There's one new entry in the /sys/power/tuxonice directory - no_flusher_thread. This entry is only useful if you've got multiple cpus/cores
column12: and then only if no_multithreaded_io is 0 (ie multithreaded I/O is enabled). What I've done is this: by default
column13: we now dedicate one thread (the CPU 0 one) to just submitting I/O. All other threads spend their time compressing pages and filling pages with the compressed data and associated metadata
column14: then queueing filled pages for the submission thread to handle. If there's only one thread or no_flusher_thread is used
column15: we go back to the old behaviour - threads compress
column16: fill pages and submit them. So... options for multicore users: 1) Single threaded operation procsetting no_multithreaded_io 1 2) Multithreaded
column17: flusher thread (default) procsetting no_multithreaded_io 0 procsetting no_flusher_thread 0 3) Multithreaded
column18: no flusher thread procsetting no_multithreaded_io 0 procsetting no_flusher_thread 1 If you give the patches a try
column19: would you please let me know how these different options perform? Regards

Therefore and the juice is  >not worth the squeeze unless the receiver actually knows the domain. >Perfect DKIM+SSP by a total stranger is relatively meaningless. > I'm asking in terms of the overall implementation. In a world where all domains are strangers the juice is definately not worth the squeeze. That is the chicken and egg of kickstarting adoption.  Is the same true where half (or pick a percentage of your choice)the domains are strangers? At what point do the benefits of checking outweigh the costs of checking? >But we've already visted that station many times in the past. > > Wietse While it may be absolutely correct with no context - relatively meaningless at a micro level until behavior starts to be examined and matched to that signature. At a macro level it may be that receivers assign a reputation of newly signing domains based on general experience with the class (or segments based on type of mail received from that class) newly signing domains. It may be that DKIM+SSP will be matched to previous mail flows by IP address or other characteristics associated with a sender. Until DKIM+SSP is in the wild it is hard to say how that will play out. If we are trying to use DKIM+SSP to directly identify ""bad"" then I'm not sure how useful it will be. There are plenty of ways for bad actors to act bad. On the other hand
column18: if DKIM+SSP allows some determination of ""good reputation"" (tied to behavior of that signing domain) - even if over time - then it may be useful in some cases. If that then enables a comparison of the two (where bad is purporting to be the good actor within certain parameters)it may be useful in other cases. It will certainly be interesting to see what happens when DKIM+SSP ""good reputation"" turns to ""bad""
column19: especially when it involves subversion of a domains own security processes. Much talk of how reputation is gained but little of it's loss. How sticky will good reputation based on DKIM+SSP or other metrics be? Without SSP
column20: how (or even why) will receivers choose to take advantage of DKIM? I'm not talking a handful of domains
column21: I'm talking more general adoption by receivers. If potential 1st party or 3rd party legitimate signers (not the bad guys) don't have some expectation as to how receivers will interpret and act on their signing
column22: how strong an incentive do they have to begin signing? I'm also assuming that their expectation has to be a positive outcome or they have a disincentive to sign. It's a given that spammers will try to use/abuse DKIM and DKIM+SSP to cloak themselves with. It's the nature of the beast. This ties into other issues surrounding mail
column23: domain host compromise and other abuse. I fully realize that even if DKIM+SSP can afford protection for certain things it doesn't protect from all bad things. That's another given.  My understanding with regard to DKIM and other authentication approaches is that the goal is to stake out defined areas and practices which can identify/protect legitimate (even if limited or only after reputation is built) mail and hopefully drive out bad actors from those areas.  So if it isn't 3PS (01) and it isn't ASP (02) then what is it that is to be identified/protected by SSP? There are at least three large receivers that are checking DKIM and assigning pass/fail to those signatures
column24: even if they may not currently be taking action on those determinations . I have to assume that there is a perceived potential benefit on their part to checking for signatures as well as checking of signatures.  Is DKIM checking sufficient in itself without SSP? How might DKIM-SSP help receivers (the 3 aforementioned as well as others) leverage their evaluation of received email whether signed (valid or not) or unsigned? He is unable to speak with the ventilator right now but he is aware and tries to write us little notes to ask for what he needs. Right before I left today he asked me to bring the laptop tomorrow. I'm sure how well that is going to work because he is not too very lucid but I at the very least I can read him everyone's get well wishes. Thank you so much for all your prayers and get well thoughts. I really appreciate it and I know Scott does too.
